changes.text: 胡适自己对来龙去脉的解释是反对单因论。他开玩笑说，历史上的意外事件往往比“单因”——经济、色欲、上帝之类——更重要：正因为这些单因对所有事件皆可解释，它们也就不可解释任何事件。就他这段经历而言，他明确把送别诗称作「意外的小事」，并说「一连串的小意外事件，逐渐地强迫我采取了这个立场」；本文把传单和湖上险些翻船引出的争论也放进这一串，这是本文的归并。把一连串小意外看作推力，是他本人的史观，不是本文的结论。

Hu's own explanation of how it all happened is that he opposed single-cause theories of history. He used to joke that accidents matter more than any monistic cause — economics, lust, God and the rest: those single causes explain everything that has ever happened, and precisely because they explain everything, they explain nothing. In this episode he explicitly called the farewell poem a small accident, and said that a chain of small accidents had gradually forced him into his position; placing the leaflet and the dispute that followed the near-capsize on the lake in that chain is this article's own grouping. Reading a chain of small accidents as the push behind his position is Hu's own view of history, not a finding of this article.

Two days later came a close call on Cayuga Lake. On July 8 Ren Hongjun, Chen Hengzhe of Vassar, Mei Guangdi, Yang Quan, Tang Yue and others were rowing on the lake when a black cloud gathered overhead, a storm broke and the rain fell; pulling for shore in a hurry they nearly capsized, and all came away soaked and dishevelled. For that band of Chinese students it was a real adventure, and Ren wrote it up in Fanhu jishi (Boating on the Lake), an old four-character-style poem he mailed to Hu for criticism. It used archaic words such as the particle yan, of the kind found in the Book of Songs — Hu had earlier written an essay on that very word — and he disliked dead diction mixed with modern language. He wrote back that the poem was bad because its wording was thoroughly incongruous, and he spoke of dead language of three thousand years ago (both paraphrased from the Chinese). Ren was indignant. More interesting was the letter that followed: Mei, his other friend at Harvard, riding to the rescue in high dudgeon. Under the influence of his conservative teacher Babbitt, Mei opposed all of Hu's radicalism to the end — language becomes poetic only after first-rate poets refine it, and the language of literature, poetry above all, must be beautified by first-rate poets and artists before it counts as poetic diction. On that ground he lashed Hu's ideas.

It appeared in New Youth in January 1917 and stirred a great response. Two Peking University professors took it seriously. Chen Duxiu, an unbending revolutionary, answered with "On Literary Revolution," publicly backing a literary revolution and saying frankly that the banner had been raised by his friend Hu Shi; he himself was raising the banner high in his friend's support. Qian Xuantong, professor of classical phonology, a master of ancient prose and a disciple of the great scholar Zhang Taiyan, wrote no article but sent Chen and Hu long letters — small criticisms, great praise — also printed in New Youth; that so eminent a classicist should sympathize buoyed their cause. Zhao Yuanren often said that Hu's vernacular poems and essays were "not vernacular enough," not the genuine spoken style ordinary people used. Hu admitted it: like a woman who had bound her feet for forty, or even twenty, years, however much she loosened the bindings she would never recover natural feet.
另一种解释是关于措辞的分工：他把“革命”换成“改良”，把结论降格为“刍议”，自己承担温和的发表风险；陈独秀随后把它高举为“文学革命”，由更激进的人去举旗。据胡适转述，陈独秀坦白说首举义旗的是胡适，他自己高张大旗作声援。这种“一人放低、一人举高”的配合，是作者从先后次序读出的一种可能，并非本文所据材料的记载。

A second reading concerns the division of labour over words. He swapped revolution for reform and demoted his conclusion to a humble opinion, taking on himself the risk of publishing moderately; Chen Duxiu then raised it as literary revolution, and a more radical man carried the flag. By Hu's report, Chen said frankly that the banner was Hu's and that he himself was raising it high in support. This doubling — one man lowering the volume, one raising it — is a possibility the author reads in the sequence, not something recorded in the material this piece relies on.

作者推断：他选择以身作则，并不只是姿态，而是把分歧改造成可检验的问题。“白话不能用之于诗”是个全称判断，理论上一首像样的白话诗就能动摇它；反之，没有诗，再多书信也只是意见相持。他把新诗集提前定名《尝试集》，等于先给自己揽下举证责任，把胜负交给一场公开、长期、别人看得见的试验。一种解释是，这也呼应了译注者唐德刚对他的定位——夹在必然与偶然之间的“实验主义者”，不肯听任事情自然演变，而要在试验中寻找方向。不过「没有“胡适”，恐怕也就没有“白话文运动”——至少运动也不会在那时就发生了」是唐德刚的评论，不是可核实的史实。

The author's inference: his decision to lead by example was not merely a pose; it converted a disagreement into a testable question. The claim that the vernacular cannot be used for poetry is a universal one, and one decent vernacular poem is enough in principle to shake it; without a poem, letters could go on forever as a standoff of opinions. By naming the collection Experiments in advance, he took on the burden of proof in advance and left the outcome to a long, open trial that others could watch. One reading is that this matches the translator-editor Tang Degang's portrait of him as a pragmatist standing between necessity and chance, unwilling to let events drift and determined to search out the right direction through experiment. Still, Tang's remark — in paraphrase, that without Hu Shi there would probably have been no Vernacular Movement, or at least it would not have happened then — is commentary, not verifiable history.
本文材料只来自一本书：胡适口述、唐德刚译注《胡适口述自传》（中国文史出版社2020年）。按唐德刚说明，这一章英文稿是从《四十自述》中《逼上梁山》那一章节译、经胡适手订后又回译成中文的，与原文多少有点出入。因此这是当事人多年后的自述，不是当时的独立记录；梅光迪、任鸿隽的反应和话语，都经胡适转述，本文不推测他们的内心。

The material here comes from one book only: Hu Shi's oral memoir, translated and annotated by Tang Degang, The Oral Memoir of Hu Shi (Chinese Literature and History Press, 2020). As Tang explains, the English draft of this chapter was abridged from the Bi shang Liangshan (Driven to Liangshan) chapter of Hu's Forty Self-Narratives, revised in Hu's own hand, then translated back into Chinese — and it differs from the original in some degree. This is therefore a participant's account given many years later, not an independent record from the time. Mei Guangdi's and Ren Hongjun's reactions and their words all reach us through Hu's retelling, and this piece does not speculate about their inner thoughts.
